texto.titulo: Walking together: effects of a volunteer-led community walking programme on blood pressure and well-being in older adults
texto.autores: R. Valdemar, T. Okonkwo-Lisle and M. Herrán
texto.abstract: Although regular walking is widely recommended for the prevention and management of hypertension in later life, comparatively little is known about whether group-based programmes delivered by community volunteers, rather than by health professionals, produce comparable benefits. This study examined the effects of a 16-week volunteer-led group walking programme on resting blood pressure and subjective well-being among community-dwelling adults aged 60 and over. A quasi-experimental design with a non-randomised comparison group was adopted in two neighbourhoods of a mid-sized city. A total of 184 participants were enrolled, of whom 171 completed the follow-up assessment. Compared with the comparison group, participants in the programme showed significantly greater reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure, as well as greater gains in well-being, whereas changes in loneliness did not reach statistical significance. Reductions in blood pressure were largest among those who attended at least 70% of the sessions. The findings suggest that volunteer-led group walking may represent a low-cost and acceptable strategy for cardiovascular health promotion in older populations, albeit one whose long-term effects remain to be established.
texto.keywords: hypertension, older adults, group walking, physical activity, well-being, community health promotion

blocos.p: Hypertension remains one of the most prevalent and, at the same time, most modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease, stroke and premature mortality in later life. Estimates drawn from population surveys in several regions suggest that between half and two thirds of adults aged 65 and over have elevated blood pressure, and that a substantial proportion of them are either unaware of the condition or fail to achieve adequate control despite pharmacological treatment (Thornquist, 2016; Adebayo-Reis et al., 2019). Given that the number of older adults is projected to grow considerably over the coming decades, the burden that uncontrolled hypertension places on health systems is expected to rise accordingly. Physical inactivity, which tends to increase with age, has been consistently identified as a contributing factor, and it is for this reason that public health guidelines have increasingly emphasised the promotion of regular, moderate-intensity activity as a complement to, rather than a substitute for, medical management. Moreover, the consequences of poorly controlled blood pressure extend beyond mortality, since hypertension is also associated with cognitive decline, loss of independence and more frequent hospital admissions, all of which carry considerable costs for families and care services.

Among the forms of activity available to older people, walking occupies a particularly favourable position. It requires no special equipment, can be undertaken in almost any setting and carries a comparatively low risk of injury, which makes it suitable for individuals who have never engaged in structured exercise. Fenwright and Ostrova (2018), in a meta-analysis of 31 trials, reported that regular walking was associated with average reductions of 3 to 5 mmHg in systolic blood pressure, an effect they described as modest at the individual level but potentially substantial when extended to whole populations. Ashcombe (2020) reached a broadly similar conclusion, albeit with the caveat that most of the trials reviewed had been conducted with middle-aged rather than older participants and had lasted less than twelve weeks. It cannot therefore be assumed that the benefits observed in those studies would be reproduced among adults in their seventies and eighties, whose physiological responses to exercise may differ. Moreover, the intensity at which older adults walk is often lower than that prescribed in trial protocols, which raises the question of whether the doses tested in younger samples are realistic for this population.

A second line of research has examined the format in which walking is undertaken. Pellegrini-Shaw (2015) argued that walking in groups offers advantages that go beyond the physical activity itself, since the regular presence of companions provides encouragement, a sense of obligation and opportunities for conversation that solitary walking does not. In a cohort of retired adults followed for one year, Dourado et al. (2021) found that those who walked in organised groups maintained their routines considerably longer than those who had been given an individual walking plan, and they attributed this difference largely to the social commitments that members developed towards one another. Lindgaard (2019), however, cautioned that the benefits of group formats are not evenly distributed: individuals with lower fitness levels may feel pressured to keep pace with faster walkers and, as a consequence, may withdraw from programmes earlier than their more active peers. Taken together, these studies suggest that the social dimension of group walking may act both as an incentive and, for some participants, as a deterrent.

Alongside its cardiovascular effects, physical activity in later life has been linked to a range of psychological outcomes, of which subjective well-being has attracted particular attention. Quintero and Hale (2017) define well-being in older adults as a multidimensional construct comprising life satisfaction, positive affect and a sense of purpose, and they distinguish it from loneliness, which they regard as a related but separate experience of perceived social deficit. Varga-Moller (2020) reported that participants in a community exercise scheme showed improvements in both outcomes after six months, whereas Nakashima-Ford (2018) found that well-being improved while loneliness remained largely unchanged, suggesting that short-term contact with others does not necessarily alter the more enduring sense of isolation experienced by some older people. The relationship between group activity and these two outcomes is thus far from settled, and it has been suggested that the duration of exposure may be as decisive as the type of activity offered (Nakashima-Ford, 2018). Measurement has added to the uncertainty, since studies have used a variety of instruments, some of which combine well-being and loneliness items in a single score and therefore cannot separate the two outcomes.

A further gap concerns the context in which interventions are delivered. The majority of the trials on which current recommendations rest were conducted in supervised settings, with sessions led by exercise physiologists or nurses and with participants recruited through clinics (Ekwueme-Brand, 2014; Fenwright & Ostrova, 2018). It is frequently assumed that the effects obtained under such conditions can be transferred to community programmes without loss, yet the latter typically operate with fewer resources, rely on volunteers with limited training and attract participants who differ in motivation and health status from those enrolled in clinical trials. Programmes led by volunteers are, admittedly, attractive to local authorities precisely because of their low cost; nonetheless, evidence regarding their effectiveness on clinical outcomes, as opposed to attendance or satisfaction, remains scarce (Lindgaard, 2019; Ashcombe, 2020). Volunteer leaders may also find it harder than professionals to adapt sessions to participants with different abilities, a difficulty that could affect both safety and attendance.

The present study was designed to address these gaps by evaluating a volunteer-led group walking programme implemented by a municipal health promotion service in the city of Calderford. Rather than testing the efficacy of walking under optimal conditions, the study sought to estimate the effects that may reasonably be expected when such a programme is delivered as part of routine community provision, with all the irregularities in attendance and leadership that this entails. Both clinical and psychosocial outcomes were considered, given that the value of community programmes for older adults is often judged by participants and providers alike in terms of enjoyment and social contact as much as in terms of measurable health gains. The evaluation was planned jointly with the municipal service, but the research team had no role in recruiting walk leaders or in deciding where and when the walks would take place.

Three research questions guided the study: (RQ1) Does participation in a 16-week volunteer-led group walking programme reduce resting systolic and diastolic blood pressure among community-dwelling adults aged 60 and over, compared with a group receiving printed advice only? (RQ2) Does participation in the programme improve subjective well-being and reduce loneliness? (RQ3) Is the magnitude of change in blood pressure related to the proportion of sessions attended? It was hypothesised that participants in the programme would show greater reductions in blood pressure and greater gains in well-being than those in the comparison group, and that changes would be largest among the most regular attenders. No directional hypothesis was formulated for loneliness, in view of the conflicting findings reported in the literature.

The study was conducted between March and July 2023 in two neighbourhoods of Calderford with comparable socioeconomic profiles and similar proportions of residents aged over 60. The programme was introduced in the northern neighbourhood, Elmsgate, while the southern neighbourhood, Brennock Vale, served as the comparison site; allocation was determined by the municipal service’s implementation schedule rather than by the researchers, which precluded randomisation. Participants were recruited through community centres, primary care noticeboards and local radio. Eligible individuals were aged 60 or over, lived independently, were able to walk unaided for at least 15 minutes and had not engaged in regular structured exercise during the previous six months. Those with uncontrolled cardiac conditions, recent surgery or a medical recommendation against moderate exercise were excluded. Recruitment materials were identical in the two neighbourhoods and described the study simply as an investigation of physical activity and health in later life, without specifying which form of activity would be offered.

A total of 184 participants were enrolled, 96 in the intervention group and 88 in the comparison group. Their mean age was 68.4 years (SD = 5.9; range 60–84), and 113 (61.4%) were women. Just over half (52.7%) reported taking at least one antihypertensive medication at baseline, a proportion that did not differ significantly between groups. Thirteen participants did not complete the follow-up assessment, seven in the intervention group and six in the comparison group, mainly because of illness, relocation or loss of interest, leaving an analytic sample of 171 (89 and 82, respectively). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the protocol was approved by the ethics committee of the Northbridge Institute of Health Sciences (protocol 2022/117). Compared with the general population of older residents in the two neighbourhoods, the sample included a slightly higher proportion of women and of people who had completed secondary education.

The intervention consisted of three walking sessions per week over 16 weeks, each lasting approximately 45 minutes, including a five-minute warm-up and a five-minute cool-down. Sessions were led by 14 volunteer walk leaders, most of them retired residents, who had completed a two-day training course covering route planning, basic first aid and strategies for encouraging participants of differing abilities. Routes of 2.5 to 4 km were designed along pavements and park paths, and walkers were divided into a ‘steady’ and a ‘brisk’ group so that no participant was obliged to keep pace with others considerably fitter than themselves. Participants in the comparison group received a printed leaflet with general recommendations on physical activity. The programme itself is now being extended to Brennock Vale, where comparison-group participants will be offered priority places in the walking groups from the spring of 2025.

Resting blood pressure was measured at baseline and at the end of week 16 by trained research assistants using a validated automated oscillometric device. After the participant had been seated quietly for five minutes, three readings were taken at one-minute intervals on the left arm, and the mean of the second and third readings was used in the analysis. Subjective well-being was assessed with the Later Life Well-being Inventory (LLWI), a 12-item self-report instrument which is composed of three subscales (life satisfaction, positive affect and sense of purpose) and has been used in several community studies with older adults (Quintero & Hale, 2017). Items are rated on a five-point scale, yielding total scores between 12 and 60, with higher scores indicating greater well-being; internal consistency in the present sample was high (Cronbach’s α = .87). Loneliness was measured with the six-item Brief Loneliness Scale (BLS; scores 6–24), on which higher scores denote greater loneliness. All measures were administered in community centres by the same team of assistants, who followed a standard script and recorded any deviations from the protocol.

Data were analysed using a per-protocol approach, that is, including only participants who completed both assessments. Between-group differences in change scores (follow-up minus baseline) were examined with independent-samples t-tests, and within-group changes with paired t-tests. Because the groups were not randomised, analyses of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusting for baseline values, age, sex and antihypertensive medication were also conducted as a sensitivity check. To address RQ3, participants in the intervention group were classified as high attenders (70% or more of the 48 sessions) or low attenders (less than 70%), and their change scores were compared. Effect sizes are reported as Cohen’s d, and the significance level was set at p < .05 (two-tailed). Missing items on the LLWI and BLS, which affected fewer than 2% of responses, were replaced by the mean of the participant’s remaining items on the same subscale.

At baseline, the two groups did not differ significantly in age, sex distribution, body mass index, medication use or any of the outcome measures (all p > .20). Mean systolic blood pressure was 142.6 mmHg (SD = 14.1) in the intervention group and 141.9 mmHg (SD = 13.7) in the comparison group, while mean diastolic values were 84.3 and 83.8 mmHg, respectively. Participants who withdrew before the follow-up assessment were slightly older than those who remained, but did not differ from them in baseline blood pressure or well-being. Mean body mass index was 27.1 in both groups, and the proportion of participants living alone was similar in Elmsgate (38.5%) and Brennock Vale (36.4%).

Table 1 shows the mean values of all outcomes at baseline and at week 16, together with the between-group differences in change. Systolic blood pressure decreased from 142.6 to 135.1 mmHg in the intervention group, a mean reduction of 7.5 mmHg, whereas in the comparison group it fell only marginally, from 141.9 to 140.3 mmHg (−1.6 mmHg). The difference in change scores between groups (−5.9 mmHg) was statistically significant, t(169) = 4.21, p < .001, d = 0.64. A smaller but nonetheless significant between-group difference was observed for diastolic pressure, which fell by 3.8 mmHg in the intervention group (from 84.3 to 80.5 mmHg) and by 0.9 mmHg in the comparison group (from 83.8 to 82.9 mmHg), a between-group difference of −2.9 mmHg, t(169) = 2.37, p = .019, d = 0.36. These results were essentially unchanged when baseline values, age, sex and medication use were controlled for in the ANCOVA models. The proportion of participants whose blood pressure fell below 140/90 mmHg rose from 41.6% to 58.4% in the intervention group, compared with an increase from 42.7% to 45.1% in the comparison group.

Table 1 also summarises the psychosocial outcomes. Mean LLWI scores in the intervention group increased from 38.2 (SD = 7.4) at baseline to 43.6 (SD = 6.9) at follow-up, while scores in the comparison group remained virtually stable (37.9 to 38.5). The between-group difference in change (4.8 points) was significant, t(169) = 3.58, p < .001, d = 0.55, and was driven chiefly by the positive affect and sense of purpose subscales, with life satisfaction showing a smaller, non-significant gain. Loneliness, by contrast, declined only slightly in the intervention group (from 13.4 to 12.6 on the BLS) and was unchanged in the comparison group (13.1 to 13.0); this difference (−0.7 points) did not reach statistical significance, t(169) = 1.82, p = .071. As shown in the final row of Table 1, the proportion of participants who reported feeling ‘often or always’ lonely fell from 22.5% to 18.0% in the intervention group, albeit from a level comparable to that of the comparison group, in which it remained at around 21% (21.3% at baseline and 20.7% at follow-up).

blocos.p: Attendance records indicated that participants in the intervention group attended a mean of 34.7 of the 48 sessions offered (72.3%). Fifty-eight participants (65.2%) were classified as high attenders and 31 (34.8%) as low attenders. Among high attenders, systolic blood pressure fell by a mean of 9.6 mmHg, compared with 3.6 mmHg among low attenders, t(87) = 3.05, p = .003. Attendance was lowest during the two weeks of unusually hot weather in June, when several sessions were cancelled or shortened, and highest in the ‘steady’ walking group, a finding which is consistent with the concern raised by Lindgaard (2019) regarding the pressure that faster walkers may place on slower ones. Low attenders most often cited family commitments, minor health problems and temporary absence from the city as reasons for missing sessions.

Exploratory analyses suggested that reductions in systolic pressure were of similar magnitude among women (−7.8 mmHg) and men (−7.0 mmHg) and among participants taking and not taking antihypertensive medication. Participants aged 75 and over (n = 17) showed a smaller mean reduction (−4.9 mmHg), although the small size of this subgroup precludes firm conclusions. Three minor adverse events were recorded during the programme, all of them falls without injury on uneven ground, and none led to withdrawal. In brief written comments collected at follow-up, participants most frequently mentioned companionship, the regularity of the schedule and the encouragement of walk leaders as reasons for continuing to attend. Several also noted that the walks had led them to visit parts of the city they had not explored for years, while a minority reported that sessions held early in the morning were difficult to reconcile with caring responsibilities.

The present findings indicate that a programme led by volunteers, operating under the ordinary constraints of community provision, produced a clinically meaningful reduction of resting systolic blood pressure among older adults. The mean between-group difference of approximately 6 mmHg is somewhat larger than the 3 to 5 mmHg reported by Fenwright and Ostrova (2018), albeit within the range of individual trials included in their review. Several factors may account for this difference. Participants were required to have been inactive for the previous six months, and it is plausible that individuals starting from a lower level of activity derive proportionally greater benefit from a given dose of walking. In addition, the relatively high baseline blood pressure of the sample may have left more room for improvement than in studies of normotensive volunteers. Given that reductions of around 5 mmHg in systolic pressure have been associated with marked declines in population stroke mortality rates (Thornquist, 2016), the magnitude of the effect observed here would appear to be of public health relevance. It should be noted, however, that the confidence interval around this estimate was relatively wide, so that a more cautious reading would place the effect towards the upper end of the range reported in previous reviews.

The improvement in well-being lends support to the view, advanced by Pellegrini-Shaw (2015), that the benefits of group walking extend beyond its physiological effects. That the gains were concentrated in positive affect and sense of purpose, rather than in life satisfaction, is perhaps unsurprising: the former two dimensions are likely to respond to the immediate experience of regular, shared activity, whereas global judgements of life satisfaction are thought to be comparatively stable in later life (Quintero & Hale, 2017). The absence of a significant effect on loneliness is more difficult to interpret. It is consistent with the findings of Nakashima-Ford (2018) but not with those of Varga-Moller (2020), whose programme lasted considerably longer than ours. One possibility is that sixteen weeks is simply insufficient for the acquaintances formed during walks to develop into the kind of relationships capable of alleviating a deeper sense of isolation. It is also possible that the Brief Loneliness Scale, which asks about relatively stable feelings over the preceding month, is less sensitive to short-term change than the well-being measure.

The dose–response relationship observed between attendance and blood pressure change strengthens the inference that the reductions were attributable to the programme rather than to regression towards the mean or to seasonal variation, although the latter cannot be entirely ruled out. It also carries practical implications. Since high attenders benefited substantially more than low attenders, efforts to sustain attendance are likely to be as important as the content of the sessions themselves. The higher attendance recorded in the ‘steady’ group suggests that offering walks at different paces, a feature which was introduced primarily for reasons of safety, may have had the additional effect of retaining participants who would otherwise have felt unable to keep up. Programmes elsewhere could readily adopt this arrangement at little or no additional cost.

From a public health perspective, the principal appeal of volunteer-led programmes lies in their potential for wide implementation. The direct costs of the programme evaluated here, consisting mainly of leader training, printed route maps and insurance, were estimated by the municipal service at approximately 46 euros per participant over the 16 weeks, a figure that compares favourably with most clinic-based alternatives. Notwithstanding these advantages, it should not be concluded that volunteer leadership can replace professional input altogether. The training of leaders, the screening of participants and the procedures for responding to adverse events all depended on the involvement of health professionals, and it is unlikely that programmes lacking such support would achieve comparable levels of safety. Community walking programmes should therefore be regarded as a complement to, and not a substitute for, the clinical management of hypertension. The reliance on volunteers also raises questions of continuity, since several leaders in the present programme indicated that they could not commit to leading walks throughout the year.

Several limitations should be borne in mind when interpreting these findings. First, and most importantly, the absence of randomisation means that the two groups cannot be regarded as equivalent with respect to unmeasured characteristics such as motivation, social networks or health literacy. Although the groups were comparable on all measured baseline variables, participants who volunteered for a programme that was about to start in their own neighbourhood may have differed from those who agreed to join a comparison group in ways that also influenced the outcomes. Second, the research assistants who measured blood pressure were aware of participants’ group allocation, which may have introduced a degree of observer bias, albeit one limited by the use of automated devices. Third, the psychosocial outcomes relied entirely on self-report, and participants in the programme may have been inclined to give favourable responses to researchers whom they associated with the walking groups. Finally, the study was conducted in a single city over a single season, and the per-protocol analysis may have overestimated the effects, given that those who withdrew were slightly older. Taken together, these limitations mean that the estimates reported here should be regarded as indicative rather than definitive.

Future research should address these limitations in several ways. Cluster-randomised trials, in which neighbourhoods rather than individuals are allocated to the programme, would allow the effects of volunteer-led walking to be estimated with greater confidence while preserving the community character of the intervention. Longer follow-up periods might reveal whether the reductions in blood pressure are maintained after the end of the structured programme and whether, over time, the social contacts formed during walks translate into reduced loneliness. Studies are also needed in more diverse settings, including rural areas and neighbourhoods with lower levels of income, where the condition of pavements, the availability of parks and perceived safety may impose additional barriers. Lastly, formal economic evaluations comparing volunteer-led and professionally led programmes would help local authorities to decide how scarce resources might best be allocated. Qualitative studies exploring why some participants stop attending would also be valuable, since the reasons for withdrawal may differ from those that motivate initial enrolment.

This study provides evidence that a volunteer-led group walking programme, delivered as part of routine municipal provision, can produce reductions in resting blood pressure among older adults that are comparable to, and in some respects larger than, those reported in more tightly controlled trials, together with improvements in subjective well-being. The programme did not, within sixteen weeks, significantly reduce loneliness, and its benefits were concentrated among those who attended regularly. These findings suggest that the value of such programmes depends less on the sophistication of their content than on their capacity to keep older people walking, week after week, in the company of others. Provided that adequate professional support for training and safety is maintained, volunteer-led walking may be regarded as a promising, low-cost complement to the clinical management of hypertension, although its long-term effects remain to be confirmed by randomised studies.

questoes.enunciado: Com base no título e no resumo, o tema do estudo reportado no texto é
alternativas: os efeitos de um programa de caminhada em grupo conduzido por profissionais de saúde sobre a pressão arterial e o bem-estar de idosos que vivem na comunidade.
os efeitos de um programa de caminhada em grupo conduzido por voluntários sobre a pressão arterial e a solidão de idosos que vivem na comunidade.
os efeitos de um programa de caminhada em grupo conduzido por voluntários sobre a pressão arterial e o bem-estar de idosos com hipertensão não controlada.
os efeitos de um programa de caminhada em grupo conduzido por voluntários sobre a pressão arterial e o bem-estar de idosos que vivem na comunidade.
a relação entre a frequência às sessões de um programa de caminhada em grupo conduzido por voluntários e a pressão arterial de idosos.
questoes.explicacao:
O resumo delimita o estudo: the effects of a 16-week volunteer-led group walking programme on resting blood pressure and subjective well-being among community-dwelling adults aged 60 and over. São quatro elementos: quem conduz (voluntários), o formato (grupo), os desfechos (pressão e bem-estar) e a população (idosos que vivem na comunidade). Só (d) mantém os quatro.

Cada distrator troca um único elemento: (a) troca quem conduz; o texto contrasta justamente community volunteers, rather than […] health professionals. (b) troca o desfecho: a solidão foi medida, mas é secundária e did not reach statistical significance; o título fala em well-being. (c) troca a população: os participantes não precisavam ser hipertensos (só 52,7% tomavam anti-hipertensivo), e quem tinha condições cardíacas não controladas foi excluído. (e) é estreito demais: a relação com a frequência é só a RQ3, uma análise complementar.
questoes.dica: Dica: Monte o tema com os elementos do título e do resumo (intervenção, quem a conduz, desfechos, população) e confira cada alternativa elemento por elemento. Quando as alternativas são quase iguais, o erro está em um só termo, muitas vezes outro termo que também aparece no texto.

(2021) found that those who walked in organised groups maintained their routines considerably longer than those who had been given an individual walking plan, and they attributed this difference largely to the social commitments that members developed towards one another” (§3) e “[…] individuals with lower fitness levels may feel pressured to keep pace with faster walkers and, as a consequence, may withdraw from programmes earlier than their more active peers” (§3) referem-se, respectivamente, a
alternativas: Dourado et al. – os participantes que caminhavam em grupos organizados – individuals with lower fitness levels.
Dourado et al. – o fato de os participantes dos grupos manterem a rotina por mais tempo – individuals with lower fitness levels.
os participantes que caminhavam em grupos organizados – Dourado et al. – Dourado et al..
os participantes que caminhavam em grupos organizados – o fato de os participantes dos grupos manterem a rotina por mais tempo – individuals with lower fitness levels.
os participantes que caminhavam em grupos organizados – o fato de os participantes dos grupos manterem a rotina por mais tempo – Dourado et al..
questoes.explicacao:
they: quem attributed (atribuiu uma causa a um resultado) são os pesquisadores, Dourado et al., sujeito de found. Os participantes dos grupos são o candidato mais próximo, mas foram eles que maintained their routines; não foram eles que interpretaram o achado.

this difference: resume a comparação da oração anterior, isto é, os que caminhavam em grupo maintained their routines considerably longer than os de plano individual. Os social commitments vêm depois e são a causa atribuída a essa diferença (attributed this difference […] to), não a diferença em si.

their: “seus pares mais ativos” só faz sentido para quem é menos ativo, ou seja, individuals with lower fitness levels, sujeito de may withdraw. Faster walkers é o substantivo mais próximo, mas não teria “pares mais ativos” do que si mesmo.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra o item 2; (c) erra os itens 1, 2 e 3; (d) erra o item 1; (e) erra os itens 1 e 3.
questoes.dica: Dica: O referente nem sempre é o substantivo mais próximo. Para cada pronome, confira número e veja qual candidato pode fazer a ação do verbo (quem pode “atribuir”? quem tem “pares mais ativos”?). Para “this/these + substantivo”, procure a ideia inteira resumida e separe-a da sua causa ou consequência.

questoes.enunciado:
Na introdução (§2–§4), os autores retomam estudos anteriores. Associe as colunas, relacionando cada autor à ideia que lhe é atribuída no texto.

  1. Fenwright and Ostrova (2018)
  2. Ashcombe (2020)
  3. Dourado et al. (2021)
  4. Lindgaard (2019)
  5. Nakashima-Ford (2018)
  • (  )Chegou a uma conclusão parecida com a de outra revisão, mas observou que os estudos analisados envolviam sobretudo adultos de meia-idade e duravam menos de três meses.
  • (  )Constatou que o contato com outras pessoas elevou o bem-estar sem alterar de modo apreciável a sensação de isolamento.
  • (  )Atribuiu a maior persistência de quem caminhava em grupo aos vínculos de compromisso criados entre os membros.
  • (  )Considerou o efeito da caminhada pequeno para cada indivíduo, porém potencialmente expressivo quando estendido a populações inteiras.
  • (  )Advertiu que as vantagens dos formatos em grupo não beneficiam todos os participantes por igual.
questoes.explicacao:
Ashcombe (2020) reached a broadly similar conclusion, albeit with the caveat that most of the trials reviewed had been conducted with middle-aged rather than older participants and had lasted less than twelve weeks (§2) → 2. A conclusão “parecida” é a de Fenwright e Ostrova, o que torna fácil trocar os dois (alternativa a).

Nakashima-Ford (2018) found that well-being improved while loneliness remained largely unchanged (§4) → 5. Lindgaard também faz uma ressalva, mas sobre aptidão física, não sobre solidão.

Dourado et al. (2021) attributed this difference largely to the social commitments that members developed towards one another (§3) → 3. Pellegrini-Shaw também fala de companhia, mas não está na lista; e Lindgaard trata dos grupos por outro ângulo (quem sai, não quem fica).

Fenwright and Ostrova (2018): an effect they described as modest at the individual level but potentially substantial when extended to whole populations (§2) → 1.

Lindgaard (2019) cautioned that the benefits of group formats are not evenly distributed (§3) → 4.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1, 2, 3, 4 e 5; (b) erra os itens 1, 2, 4 e 5; (c) erra os itens 3 e 4; (d) erra os itens 1 e 5.
questoes.dica: Dica: Comece pelos itens parafraseados que guardam uma ideia rara (uma ressalva sobre a amostra, uma distinção entre bem-estar e solidão). Desconfie de pares de autores do mesmo parágrafo que concordam entre si: o detalhe que os separa costuma estar na oração da ressalva (albeit, however, whereas).

questoes.enunciado: A função do segmento destacado em “Programmes led by volunteers are, admittedly, attractive to local authorities precisely because of their low cost; nonetheless, evidence regarding their effectiveness on clinical outcomes […] remains scarce” (§5) é
alternativas: admitir um ponto favorável aos programas antes de apresentar uma ressalva.
opor o baixo custo dos programas à escassez de evidências sobre sua eficácia.
realçar que o baixo custo é exatamente o motivo do interesse das autoridades.
atenuar o compromisso dos autores, atribuindo a avaliação às autoridades locais.
retomar uma constatação, feita antes no parágrafo, sobre a falta de evidências.
questoes.explicacao:
Admittedly (“é verdade que”, “reconhece-se que”) marca uma concessão: os autores aceitam um ponto a favor (o baixo custo torna os programas atraentes) para, em seguida, fazer a ressalva com nonetheless.

(b) descreve a função de nonetheless, que é quem estabelece o contraste; admittedly só prepara esse contraste. (c) é a função de precisely (“justamente”), outra palavra do trecho. (d) confunde concessão com distanciamento: os autores assumem o ponto como seu, não o atribuem às autoridades (elas são quem acha os programas atraentes, não quem faz a afirmação). (e) não há retomada: a falta de evidências aparece só depois de admittedly.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para achar a função de um advérbio de frase, isole-o dos outros marcadores do mesmo trecho: em “X, admittedly, …; nonetheless, Y”, cada palavra tem um papel (conceder, contrastar, enfatizar). Pergunte o que mudaria se só aquela palavra fosse retirada.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa que NÃO faz parte das perguntas de pesquisa apresentadas no parágrafo 7.
alternativas: Comparar a queda da pressão sistólica e da diastólica de repouso entre os participantes do programa e um grupo que recebeu só orientações impressas.
Verificar se a participação no programa diminui a solidão dos participantes.
Verificar se a magnitude da queda da pressão arterial varia conforme a idade dos participantes.
Verificar se a redução da pressão é maior entre quem compareceu a uma parcela maior das sessões.
Verificar se a participação no programa melhora o bem-estar subjetivo.
questoes.explicacao:
As três perguntas do §7 são: RQ1, a redução da pressão sistólica e diastólica compared with a group receiving printed advice only → (a); RQ2, improve subjective well-being and reduce loneliness → (e) e (b); RQ3, Is the magnitude of change in blood pressure related to the proportion of sessions attended? → (d), parafraseada.

(c) é o intruso: a diferença por idade aparece só nas análises exploratórias do §17 (Participants aged 75 and over […] showed a smaller mean reduction), não nas perguntas de pesquisa. A armadilha está em (b): para a solidão os autores não formularam hipótese (No directional hypothesis was formulated for loneliness), mas ela faz parte da RQ2. Não ter hipótese não é o mesmo que não ser pergunta de pesquisa.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em questões de NÃO, delimite o trecho pedido e confira cada alternativa nele, não no texto todo. O intruso costuma ser verdadeiro em outra seção (resultados exploratórios, discussão). Separe também pergunta de pesquisa de hipótese: uma pergunta pode existir sem hipótese.

questoes.enunciado:
Sobre o método, indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresentam os parágrafos 8 a 10.

  • (  )Eram elegíveis pessoas de 60 anos ou mais que vivessem de forma independente, conseguissem caminhar sem ajuda por ao menos 15 minutos e tivessem praticado exercício estruturado nos seis meses anteriores.
  • (  )A randomização foi inviável porque a ordem de implantação do programa nos bairros foi decidida pelo serviço municipal, e não pela equipe de pesquisa.
  • (  )As caminhadas eram guiadas por 14 voluntários, em boa parte moradores aposentados, preparados em um curso de dois dias.
  • (  )Dos 184 inscritos, 13 não fizeram a avaliação final: sete do grupo de comparação e seis do grupo de intervenção.
alternativas: A – A – A – A
D – D – A – D
A – D – D – A
A – A – D – A
D – A – A – D
questoes.explicacao:
1 (D): a lista de critérios está quase toda certa, mas o último é o oposto: had not engaged in regular structured exercise during the previous six months (§8).

2 (A): paráfrase de allocation was determined by the municipal service’s implementation schedule rather than by the researchers, which precluded randomisation (§8).

3 (A): paráfrase de 14 volunteer walk leaders, most of them retired residents, who had completed a two-day training course (§10).

4 (D): o total (13) está certo, mas os grupos estão trocados: seven in the intervention group and six in the comparison group (§9).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1 e 4; (b) erra o item 2; (c) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (d) erra os itens 1, 3 e 4.
questoes.dica: Dica: Nos itens de A/D, divida cada afirmação em partes (quem, quantos, onde, em que grupo) e confira uma por uma. Um item parafraseado com outras palavras pode estar certo; um item que copia o texto pode esconder um único detalhe trocado (um “não” que sumiu, dois números invertidos).

questoes.enunciado: Os segmentos destacados em “[…] 14 volunteer walk leaders, most of them retired residents, who had completed a two-day training course […]” (§10), “[…] walkers were divided into a ‘steady’ and a ‘brisk’ group […]” (§10), “The programme itself is now being extended to Brennock Vale […]” (§10) e “[…] comparison-group participants will be offered priority places in the walking groups […]” (§10) estão, respectivamente, nos seguintes tempos e vozes verbais:
alternativas: passado perfeito, voz ativa – passado simples, voz passiva – presente contínuo, voz passiva – futuro simples, voz passiva.
passado perfeito, voz passiva – passado simples, voz ativa – presente contínuo, voz ativa – futuro simples, voz ativa.
passado perfeito, voz ativa – passado simples, voz ativa – presente contínuo, voz ativa – futuro simples, voz passiva.
passado perfeito, voz passiva – passado simples, voz passiva – presente contínuo, voz passiva – futuro simples, voz passiva.
passado perfeito, voz ativa – passado simples, voz ativa – presente contínuo, voz ativa – futuro simples, voz ativa.
questoes.explicacao:
had completed: had + particípio = passado perfeito; os líderes fizeram o curso (sujeito agente) → voz ativa. Não há been, então não é passiva.

were divided: were + particípio = passado simples, voz passiva (os caminhantes foram divididos por alguém).

is now being extended: is + being + particípio = presente contínuo, voz passiva (o programa “está sendo ampliado”). O -ing leva a pensar em voz ativa, mas é being + particípio que forma a passiva; o advérbio now no meio não muda a estrutura.

will be offered: will + be + particípio = futuro simples, voz passiva (“receberão a oferta de vagas”). O sujeito (participants) recebe a ação; não é ele quem oferece.

Nas alternativas erradas: (b) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (c) erra os itens 2 e 3; (d) erra o item 1; (e) erra os itens 2, 3 e 4.
questoes.dica: Dica: Passiva = forma de be (am/is/are/was/were/been/being/be) + particípio. Para nomear o tempo, olhe o primeiro auxiliar: is being + particípio = presente contínuo passivo; will be + particípio = futuro passivo; had + particípio (sem been) = passado perfeito ativo. Advérbios no meio (now, already) não alteram a análise.

questoes.enunciado: Com base na Tabela 1, é correto afirmar que
alternativas: no grupo de comparação, a pressão sistólica média passou de 142,6 para 135,1 mmHg ao longo das 16 semanas.
a diferença entre os grupos na variação da pressão diastólica foi cerca de metade da observada na sistólica, mas também significativa.
no início do estudo, a parcela de participantes com pressão abaixo de 140/90 mmHg era maior no grupo de intervenção.
o bem-estar (LLWI) subiu 5,4 pontos no grupo de intervenção, e essa foi também a diferença de variação entre os grupos.
a solidão (BLS) caiu mais no grupo de intervenção do que no de comparação, uma diferença estatisticamente significativa.
questoes.explicacao:
(b) correta: na coluna Between-group difference in change, a pressão diastólica tem −2,9 mmHg e a sistólica −5,9 mmHg (cerca de metade), e o p da diastólica é .019, abaixo de .05. O texto confirma: A smaller but nonetheless significant between-group difference was observed for diastolic pressure (§14).

(a) troca de coluna: 142,6 → 135,1 são os valores do grupo de intervenção; no grupo de comparação a sistólica foi de 141,9 para 140,3 mmHg.

(c) comparação invertida: no início, 41,6% (intervenção) contra 42,7% (comparação), ou seja, a parcela era ligeiramente menor no grupo de intervenção.

(d) leitura apressada: 43,6 − 38,2 = 5,4 é a variação dentro do grupo de intervenção; a diferença de variação entre os grupos, na última coluna, é +4,8, porque o grupo de comparação também subiu 0,6.

(e) diferença não significativa tratada como significativa: a queda na BLS foi maior no grupo de intervenção (−0,8 contra −0,1), mas p = .071, acima de .05 (this difference […] did not reach statistical significance, §15).
questoes.dica: Dica: Antes de julgar as alternativas, identifique na tabela o que é cada coluna (grupo, momento, diferença, p) e leia a nota. Depois confira em cada alternativa três coisas: a célula certa (linha e coluna), o sentido da comparação (maior × menor) e se o p está abaixo do nível de significância adotado no método.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa que apresenta uma informação FALSA de acordo com o texto.
alternativas: Foram feitas três leituras da pressão em repouso, e a média das três foi a medida usada na análise (§11).
Pouco mais da metade dos inscritos já tomava algum anti-hipertensivo no início, proporção semelhante nos dois grupos (§9).
Por não haver sorteio dos grupos, as análises foram refeitas com ajuste por valores iniciais, idade, sexo e medicação (§12).
A frequência foi mais baixa nas duas semanas de calor fora do comum em junho, quando sessões foram canceladas ou encurtadas (§16).
Os participantes com 75 anos ou mais tiveram queda sistólica menor, mas o tamanho do subgrupo impede conclusões firmes (§17).
questoes.explicacao:
(a) é a falsa: de fato foram três leituras, mas a análise usou apenas a média da segunda e da terceira: three readings were taken at one-minute intervals on the left arm, and the mean of the second and third readings was used in the analysis (§11).

As demais são verdadeiras. (b) Just over half (52.7%) reported taking at least one antihypertensive medication at baseline, a proportion that did not differ significantly between groups (§9). (c) Because the groups were not randomised, analyses of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusting for baseline values, age, sex and antihypertensive medication were also conducted (§12). (d) Attendance was lowest during the two weeks of unusually hot weather in June, when several sessions were cancelled or shortened (§16). (e) Participants aged 75 and over (n = 17) showed a smaller mean reduction (−4.9 mmHg), although the small size of this subgroup precludes firm conclusions (§17).
questoes.dica: Dica: Na questão da informação falsa, as quatro verdadeiras costumam vir parafraseadas, e a falsa costuma ter quase tudo certo, com um único detalhe trocado (um número, um quantificador, “todos” × “alguns”). Vá ao parágrafo indicado e confira cada elemento da afirmação, não só o assunto.

questoes.enunciado: O segmento destacado em “Given that reductions of around 5 mmHg in systolic pressure have been associated with marked declines in population stroke mortality rates (Thornquist, 2016) […]” (§18) pode ser traduzido, no contexto em que é empregado, por
alternativas: taxas populacionais de AVC e de mortalidade.
mortalidade da população por taxas de AVC.
taxas de mortalidade por AVC na população.
taxas de AVC na mortalidade da população.
população com taxas de mortalidade por AVC.
questoes.explicacao:
Em inglês, o núcleo de uma sequência de substantivos é o último: rates (taxas). Os anteriores o modificam da direita para a esquerda: mortality rates (taxas de mortalidade) → stroke mortality rates (taxas de mortalidade por AVC) → population stroke mortality rates (… na população).

(a) desmembra stroke e mortality como duas taxas separadas (“e”). (b) e (e) tomam como núcleo mortality e population, palavras que vêm antes. (d) inverte a relação entre stroke e mortality, fazendo de stroke o modificador direto de rates.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em substantivos empilhados, ache o núcleo (a última palavra) e traduza de trás para frente, ligando cada modificador ao que vem à sua direita: A B C D → “D de C de B de A”, ajustando as preposições (de, por, em). Não acrescente “e” entre modificadores.

questoes.enunciado: No segmento “Since high attenders benefited substantially more than low attenders, efforts to sustain attendance are likely to be as important as the content of the sessions themselves. The higher attendance recorded in the ‘steady’ group suggests that offering walks at different paces, a feature which was introduced primarily for reasons of safety, may have had the additional effect of retaining participants who would otherwise have felt unable to keep up. Programmes elsewhere could readily adopt this arrangement at little or no additional cost” (§20), o segmento destacado refere-se
alternativas: à retenção de quem, de outro modo, não acompanharia o ritmo.
à adoção de medidas de segurança durante as caminhadas.
aos esforços para manter a frequência dos participantes.
à maior frequência registrada no grupo ‘steady’.
à oferta de caminhadas em ritmos diferentes.
questoes.explicacao:
This arrangement (“esse arranjo”, “essa forma de organização”) resume algo que um programa pode adotar: offering walks at different paces, isto é, dividir os caminhantes em grupos de ritmos diferentes.

(a) é o efeito do arranjo (the additional effect of retaining participants), não o arranjo. (b) é a razão pela qual ele foi criado (introduced primarily for reasons of safety). (c) aparece na frase anterior, mas “esforços” é um objetivo geral, não uma medida concreta que se adota. (d) é o resultado observado que serviu de indício (The higher attendance recorded in the ‘steady’ group suggests that…).
questoes.dica: Dica: Quando “this/these + substantivo” resume uma ideia anterior, use o substantivo como filtro: um arrangement é algo que se organiza e se adota; um finding é algo que se observa; a concern é uma preocupação. Depois, descarte a causa, o efeito e o indício que aparecem em volta.

questoes.enunciado: Em “Notwithstanding these advantages, it should not be concluded that volunteer leadership can replace professional input altogether” (§21), o conector sublinhado pode ser substituído, sem alteração de sentido, por
alternativas: Owing to
Instead of
Despite
Along with
Following
questoes.explicacao:
Notwithstanding = “apesar de”, “não obstante”: relação de concessão. Os autores reconhecem as vantagens (baixo custo, ampla implementação, ditas logo antes) e, mesmo assim, recusam a conclusão de que voluntários substituem profissionais. Despite these advantages mantém exatamente esse sentido.

(a) Owing to (“devido a”) inverteria a lógica: as vantagens passariam a ser a causa de não concluir algo. (b) Instead of (“em vez de”) indica substituição, e a ideia de “substituir” aparece na frase (replace), o que torna a troca tentadora. (d) Along with (“junto com”) indica adição. (e) Following (“após”, “em seguida a”) indica tempo ou consequência.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para testar uma substituição, reescreva a frase com a alternativa e veja se a relação continua a mesma (causa, concessão, adição, tempo). Conectores de concessão formais: notwithstanding, despite, in spite of, albeit, even though. Cuidado com as alternativas que repetem uma ideia da própria frase.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa cujo segmento sublinhado expressa o menor grau de certeza dos autores em relação ao que afirmam.
alternativas: “The present findings <u>indicate</u> that a programme led by volunteers […] produced a clinically meaningful reduction of resting systolic blood pressure among older adults” (§18).
“[…] efforts to sustain attendance <u>are likely to</u> be as important as the content of the sessions themselves” (§20).
“[…] it is <u>unlikely</u> that programmes lacking such support would achieve comparable levels of safety” (§21).
“Longer follow-up periods <u>might</u> reveal whether the reductions in blood pressure are maintained […]” (§23).
“Cluster-randomised trials […] <u>would</u> allow the effects of volunteer-led walking to be estimated with greater confidence […]” (§23).
questoes.explicacao:
Might expressa a possibilidade mais fraca: os autores não sabem se acompanhamentos mais longos vão revelar algo; apenas levantam a hipótese.

(a) indicate apresenta um resultado com segurança, apoiado nos dados. (b) are likely to = “provavelmente”: certeza alta, embora não total. (c) é a armadilha: unlikely fala de algo improvável, mas os autores estão bastante seguros de que programas sem apoio profissional não atingiriam o mesmo nível de segurança. Baixa probabilidade do fato não é baixa certeza do autor. (e) would descreve com confiança a consequência de um ensaio, se ele for feito.
questoes.dica: Dica: Ordene os modalizadores numa escala: will/cannot/indicate (alta) → are likely to/unlikely (provável ou improvável, com segurança) → may/could (possível) → might (possibilidade remota). Pergunte o quanto o autor está seguro, e não se o conteúdo é positivo ou negativo.

questoes.enunciado: Com base no segmento “the per-protocol analysis may have overestimated the effects, given that those who withdrew were slightly older” (§22), pode-se inferir que
alternativas: os participantes que desistiram tinham, no início, pressão arterial mais alta do que os que permaneceram.
os autores supõem que os desistentes, se tivessem ficado, tenderiam a obter benefícios menores que os demais.
os efeitos estimados no estudo são, com certeza, maiores do que os efeitos reais do programa.
os idosos mais velhos tendem, em geral, a abandonar programas de caminhada em grupo antes dos mais novos.
a análise por protocolo deixou de fora os participantes mais velhos que haviam sido inscritos no estudo.
questoes.explicacao:
(b) correta: a idade dos desistentes só serve de motivo para uma possível superestimação se os autores pressupõem que pessoas mais velhas respondem menos ao programa. Essa premissa não está escrita no §22, mas é coerente com o §17 (Participants aged 75 and over […] showed a smaller mean reduction). Como a análise incluiu só quem completou as duas avaliações, perder quem tenderia a melhorar menos eleva a média.

(a) contradiz o texto: os desistentes did not differ from them in baseline blood pressure or well-being (§13).

(c) generaliza demais: may have overestimated expressa possibilidade, não certeza.

(d) generaliza demais: o trecho fala dos desistentes deste estudo, sem afirmar uma tendência geral dos idosos em qualquer programa.

(e) leitura apressada: a análise por protocolo excluiu quem não completou as avaliações (including only participants who completed both assessments, §12), e não os mais velhos em si; o fato de os desistentes serem um pouco mais velhos é só uma característica desse grupo.
questoes.dica: Dica: Uma inferência é o que o trecho autoriza sem dizer com todas as letras: pergunte que premissa é necessária para o argumento fazer sentido. Descarte as alternativas que trocam possibilidade por certeza, que estendem o caso a “em geral”, que contradizem outro parágrafo ou que só remontam as palavras do trecho com outro sentido.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere as afirmações a seguir sobre a discussão (§18–§21).

I - A diferença média de cerca de 6 mmHg entre os grupos supera a faixa relatada na meta-análise de 31 ensaios, mas fica dentro da variação dos ensaios individuais que ela reuniu (§18).II - Os autores sugerem que o efeito sobre a solidão pode não ter aparecido porque o programa de Varga-Moller (2020), que obteve esse efeito, foi mais curto que o deles (§19).III - A divisão em ritmos diferentes foi criada sobretudo para manter os participantes no programa e acabou trazendo também ganhos de segurança (§20).IV - Treinamento dos líderes, mapas impressos dos percursos e seguro compõem a maior parte do custo direto estimado em cerca de 46 euros por participante (§21).

Está(ão) correta(s)
alternativas: apenas I e IV.
apenas I, II e IV.
apenas II e III.
apenas I e III.
apenas III e IV.
questoes.explicacao:
I (correta): The mean between-group difference of approximately 6 mmHg is somewhat larger than the 3 to 5 mmHg reported by Fenwright and Ostrova (2018), albeit within the range of individual trials included in their review (§18).

II (falsa): a duração está invertida: o programa de Varga-Moller lasted considerably longer than ours (§19). É justamente por isso que os autores levantam a hipótese de que sixteen weeks is simply insufficient.

III (falsa): a relação entre motivo e efeito está invertida: os ritmos diferentes foram introduced primarily for reasons of safety e tiveram the additional effect of retaining participants (§20).

IV (correta): paráfrase de The direct costs of the programme evaluated here, consisting mainly of leader training, printed route maps and insurance, were estimated by the municipal service at approximately 46 euros per participant (§21).

Assim, só (a) reúne I e IV sem incluir II ou III; (b) inclui II, (c) exclui as duas corretas, (d) inclui III e exclui IV, (e) inclui III e exclui I.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em afirmações I–IV, julgue cada uma isoladamente antes de olhar as alternativas. As falsas costumam trocar a direção de uma comparação (mais longo × mais curto) ou inverter causa e consequência (o motivo principal × o efeito adicional).

questoes.enunciado: Considerando sua estrutura e seus objetivos, o texto constitui um exemplar de
alternativas: artigo de revisão, que sintetiza estudos anteriores sobre programas de caminhada e hipertensão em idosos para apontar lacunas na literatura.
relato de caso, que descreve em detalhe a implantação de um programa municipal de caminhada em um bairro e a experiência de seus voluntários.
revisão sistemática com metanálise, que reúne ensaios sobre caminhada e pressão arterial em idosos e estima o efeito médio das intervenções.
artigo empírico, que relata um estudo quase experimental com dados coletados pelos autores sobre os efeitos de um programa de caminhada.
ensaio de opinião, que defende a ampliação de programas de caminhada guiados por voluntários como política de saúde pública de baixo custo.
questoes.explicacao:
O texto relata uma pesquisa própria, com a estrutura típica do artigo empírico: Method, Results, Discussion, Limitations and Future Research e Conclusion. O resumo anuncia o desenho (A quasi-experimental design with a non-randomised comparison group was adopted); o §8 mostra a coleta pelos próprios autores (Participants were recruited through community centres, primary care noticeboards and local radio); o §9 traz a amostra (A total of 184 participants were enrolled); o §14 apresenta resultados numéricos e testes estatísticos (a mean reduction of 7.5 mmHg, t(169) = 4.21, p < .001); e o §22 discute limitações do próprio estudo (the absence of randomisation means that the two groups cannot be regarded as equivalent). Por isso (d).

(a) confunde a parte com o todo: só a introdução (§1–§5) revisa estudos anteriores, como Fenwright and Ostrova (2018), para chegar às lacunas que o estudo vai preencher (The present study was designed to address these gaps, §6). (c) também se apoia em leitura apressada: a metanálise de 31 ensaios é de outros autores, citada no §2; o texto não reúne nem combina estudos. (b) falha porque o estudo não descreve um caso isolado: compara 96 participantes do grupo de intervenção com 88 de um grupo de comparação em outro bairro, com medidas antes e depois. (e) falha porque, embora a discussão comente o apelo do programa para a saúde pública (§21), essa avaliação se apoia nos dados coletados e vem com ressalvas (its long-term effects remain to be confirmed); o objetivo do texto é relatar e interpretar um estudo, não defender uma posição.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para identificar o gênero, olhe a estrutura e a origem dos dados. Seções de método e resultados, participantes recrutados, números e testes estatísticos e limitações do próprio estudo indicam artigo empírico. Uma revisão discute estudos de outros autores do começo ao fim; não basta a introdução fazer isso. Desconfie da alternativa que descreve bem apenas uma parte do texto.
